sql_threads.py:73-89. Cap: threads are only created inside the lock when self._workers < self._max_workers (79-83), and the count only increases, so the pool never has more than SQL_WORKER_THREADS (8) threads and at most 8 calls run at once. Excess items sit in the SimpleQueue (75) until a worker's loop (92-97) takes them. Debug log: when no idle token is available and the pool is at the cap, logger.debug is reached (85-88). Input traced: a submit that spawns the last worker returns at 84 without logging, which is right because a thread is available. A worker that finishes an item and steals a queued item via get_nowait can leave a stale idle token. That can cause a spurious debug log or an extra spawn under the cap, but never exceeds the cap or loses a queued call. Caveat: a call that spawns a new worker finds no idle thread but is not logged, so the docstring wording is slightly loose. It is accurate for the all-busy case.

sql_threads.py:73-75 creates bare Future(); :98-104 calls set_running_or_notify_cancel() before running and set_result/set_exception only when it returns True (so a cancelled future is never resolved, avoiding InvalidStateError); :128 add_done_callback; :126 asyncio.wrap_future(future). The stdlib documents set_running_or_notify_cancel as for Executor implementations (this class is one, a custom executor-like pool) and tests; the docs also say Futures are normally created by Executor.submit, a caveat that does not change behavior, since custom executors routinely do this. asyncio.wrap_future accepts concurrent.futures.Future and propagates cancel (cancel() fails harmlessly on a running future). Based on stdlib contract knowledge; CPython source not in the view.

sql_threads.py:126-129 awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future). In CPython, wrap_future uses _chain_future, which on cancellation of the asyncio future calls cancel() on the concurrent future, and the awaiting caller gets CancelledError. A concurrent Future in RUNNING state returns False from cancel() and stays running. The worker (sql_threads.py:98-104) set_running_or_notify_cancel() before calling, so a call that was already running later gets set_result/set_exception, and the done callback added at line 128 fires then (lines 111-118 log the exception). If the call was still pending, cancel succeeds and the callback fires immediately with cancelled() True and returns quietly; add_done_callback on an already-done future runs immediately. Based on my knowledge of CPython semantics; the CPython source was not read in this environment.

sql_threads.py:81 creates workers with daemon=True. CPython (3.9+) concurrent/futures/thread.py registers _python_exit via threading._register_atexit, which sets _shutdown and joins every thread in _threads_queues regardless of shutdown(wait=False); ThreadPoolExecutor workers are non-daemon. threading._shutdown joins only non-daemon threads, so daemon workers are not joined. The docstring claim matches this. I am relying on knowledge of CPython source, not a file read in the view. Absolute-claim input: shutdown(wait=False) followed by a stuck worker, where the executor's atexit join still blocks.

tests/unit/test_sql_runner_event_loop.py:33-36,39-53. The docstring says a blocked loop allows no ticks and a free one about SLOW_S/TICK_S (0.4/0.02 = 20). Blocked case: heartbeat only advances when the loop is free. If the driver call blocked the loop for SLOW_S, no sleep(TICK_S) could complete, so ticks stays 0 (< MIN_TICKS=5). Free case: the driver call runs on a worker thread, so the loop is free during the 0.4 s sleep and the heartbeat ticks about 20 times. MIN_TICKS=5 leaves a 4x margin: it fails only if the average tick interval exceeds about 80 ms, which needs extreme scheduler starvation. Trace of the absolute-claim input (a loaded runner firing fewer than 5 ticks): that would need the average tick interval to exceed about 80 ms, which a loaded CI runner can only produce under extreme starvation. All three runners define `async def run_sql` (postgres sql_runner.py:106, sqlite:73, mysql:73) and each does `return await run_blocking_sql(self._run_sql_blocking, args)` (postgres:124, sqlite:92, mysql:91), with the driver work in the sync `_run_sql_blocking`. Absolute-claim input traced: a runner calling the driver directly inside the coroutine. Sqlite's run_sql body (lines 73-92) only delegates, and sqlite3.connect and the cursor work sit in the sync helper (94+). The postgres and mysql run_sql bodies are likewise a single delegating return line. So the docstring's premise holds: run_sql is a coroutine, and a direct blocking driver call in it would block the single event loop (sql_threads.py:6-8 states the same). The docstring is accurate.

The head fixes the prior finding. sql_threads.py:126-129 awaits asyncio.wrap_future(future); on CancelledError it calls future.add_done_callback(_log_failure_after_cancel) and re-raises. Cancelling the wrapper calls concurrent Future.cancel(), which returns False for a running call, so the future stays live. _run (98-104) then calls set_exception when the driver raises, and the callback logs a warning with type(exc).__name__ (111-118). If the future has already finished, add_done_callback runs the callback immediately. A call still queued gets cancelled, set_running_or_notify_cancel returns False, and the callback returns on future.cancelled(). The callback is attached only on the cancel path, which matches the claim.
